questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Chemical Thermodynamics & Phase Equilibria (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: For one mole of a van der Waals gas obeying $\left(P + \frac{a}{V_m^2}\right)(V_m - b) = RT$, the internal pressure $\pi_T = \left(\frac{\partial U_m}{\partial V_m}\right)_T$ is equal to:
questions.explanationEn: Using the thermodynamic equation of state $\pi_T = \left(\frac{\partial U_m}{\partial V_m}\right)_T = T\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_{V_m} - P$. For a van der Waals gas, $P = \frac{RT}{V_m - b} - \frac{a}{V_m^2}$, so $\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_{V_m} = \frac{R}{V_m - b}$. Substituting gives $\pi_T = \frac{RT}{V_m - b} - \left(\frac{RT}{V_m - b} - \frac{a}{V_m^2}\right) = \frac{a}{V_m^2}$.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Chemical Thermodynamics & Phase Equilibria (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: A crystalline solid composed of linear asymmetric molecules $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ can freeze with two equally probable end-to-end orientations ($\text{NNO}$ or $\text{ONN}$) at $0\text{ K}$. The theoretical residual molar entropy of solid $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ at $0\text{ K}$ is:
questions.explanationEn: By the Boltzmann entropy formula, the residual molar entropy is $S_0 = k_B \ln W = k_B \ln(2^{N_A}) = N_A k_B \ln 2 = R\ln 2$ (approximately $5.76\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$), since each of the $N_A$ molecules has $2$ equally likely frozen-in orientations at $0\text{ K}$.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Chemical Thermodynamics & Phase Equilibria (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: For an endothermic chemical reaction with temperature-independent standard reaction enthalpy $\Delta_r H^\circ > 0$, a plot of $\ln K$ versus $1/T$ is a straight line with:
optionsEn: Positive slope equal to $\Delta_r H^\circ / R$
Negative slope equal to $-\Delta_r H^\circ / R$
Negative slope equal to $-\Delta_r G^\circ / R$
questions.explanationEn: From the integrated van't Hoff equation $\ln K = -\frac{\Delta_r H^\circ}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T}\right) + \frac{\Delta_r S^\circ}{R}$, plotting $\ln K$ against $1/T$ gives a straight line with slope $-\frac{\Delta_r H^\circ}{R}$. Since $\Delta_r H^\circ > 0$ for an endothermic reaction, the slope is negative.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Chemical Thermodynamics & Phase Equilibria (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: According to the Ehrenfest classification of phase transitions, a second-order phase transition is characterized by:
optionsEn: Discontinuous first derivatives of $G$ ($S$ and $V$) and finite latent heat
Continuous $G$, $S$, and $V$, but discontinuous second derivatives of $G$ ($C_p$, $\alpha$, $\kappa_T$)
Discontinuous chemical potential $\mu$ across the phase boundary
Zero change in heat capacity $C_p$ and non-zero volume change $\Delta V$
questions.explanationEn: In Ehrenfest's classification, an $n$-th order phase transition has continuous $(n-1)$-th derivatives of the Gibbs free energy $G$ and discontinuous $n$-th derivatives. Therefore, a second-order transition has continuous $G$, $S = -(\partial G/\partial T)_P$, and $V = (\partial G/\partial P)_T$ (hence zero latent heat and zero $\Delta V$), while $C_p = -T(\partial^2 G/\partial T^2)_P$, $\alpha$, and $\kappa_T$ are discontinuous.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Chemical Thermodynamics & Phase Equilibria (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: For any homogeneous single-phase substance, the difference between molar heat capacities $C_{p,m} - C_{V,m}$ is expressed in terms of the thermal expansion coefficient $\alpha$ and isothermal compressibility $\kappa_T$ as:
questions.explanationEn: The general thermodynamic relation is $C_{p,m} - C_{V,m} = T\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_{V_m}\left(\frac{\partial V_m}{\partial T}\right)_P$. Using $\alpha = \frac{1}{V_m}\left(\frac{\partial V_m}{\partial T}\right)_P$, $\kappa_T = -\frac{1}{V_m}\left(\frac{\partial V_m}{\partial P}\right)_T$, and the cyclic rule $\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_{V_m} = \frac{\alpha}{\kappa_T}$, we obtain $C_{p,m} - C_{V,m} = \frac{TV_m \alpha^2}{\kappa_T}$.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Chemical Thermodynamics & Phase Equilibria (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following statements regarding the Joule-Thomson (throttling) expansion of a gas is/are CORRECT?
optionsEn: The process occurs at constant enthalpy ($\Delta H = 0$).
For an ideal gas, the Joule-Thomson coefficient $\mu_{\text{JT}}$ is identically zero.
If $\mu_{\text{JT}} > 0$, the gas cools upon throttling to a lower pressure.
The process is thermodynamically reversible ($\Delta S = 0$).
questions.explanationEn: Joule-Thomson throttling through a porous plug is an adiabatic, irreversible process at constant enthalpy ($\Delta H = 0$, $\Delta S > 0$, so D is false). For an ideal gas, $H$ depends only on $T$, so $\mu_{\text{JT}} = (\partial T/\partial P)_H = 0$. Since $dP < 0$ during expansion, $\mu_{\text{JT}} > 0$ implies $dT < 0$, i.e., cooling.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Chemical Thermodynamics & Phase Equilibria (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Consider the one-component $P$-$T$ phase diagram of $\text{CO}_2$, whose triple point is at $5.11\text{ atm}$ and $216.6\text{ K}$, and critical point is at $72.8\text{ atm}$ and $304.1\text{ K}$. Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?
optionsEn: At $1\text{ atm}$, solid $\text{CO}_2$ sublimes directly to gas without melting.
The solid-liquid coexistence curve of $\text{CO}_2$ has a positive slope ($dP/dT > 0$).
Liquid $\text{CO}_2$ can exist stably at $1\text{ atm}$ if cooled to $200\text{ K}$.
Above $304.1\text{ K}$ and $72.8\text{ atm}$, $\text{CO}_2$ exists as a supercritical fluid.
questions.explanationEn: Because the triple point pressure ($5.11\text{ atm}$) exceeds $1\text{ atm}$, liquid $\text{CO}_2$ cannot exist stably at $1\text{ atm}$ at any temperature (C is false); solid $\text{CO}_2$ sublimes directly at $1\text{ atm}$ (A is true). Solid $\text{CO}_2$ is denser than liquid $\text{CO}_2$ ($\Delta_{\text{fus}} V_m > 0$), so $dP/dT > 0$ (B is true). Above the critical temperature and pressure, $\text{CO}_2$ forms a supercritical fluid (D is true).

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Chemical Thermodynamics & Phase Equilibria (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: One mole of $\text{He}(\text{g})$ and $3\text{ mol}$ of $\text{Ar}(\text{g})$, both at $298\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ bar}$, are mixed isothermally and isobarically. Assuming ideal gas behavior, the entropy of mixing ($\Delta_{\text{mix}} S$, in $\text{J K}^{-1}$, rounded off to two decimal places) is _______. (Given: $R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$)

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Chemical Thermodynamics & Phase Equilibria (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: A solution is prepared by dissolving $15.0\text{ g}$ of urea (molar mass $= 60.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, non-electrolyte) in $250\text{ g}$ of water. Taking $K_f = 1.86\text{ K kg mol}^{-1}$ for water, the freezing point depression ($\Delta T_f$, in $\text{K}$, rounded off to two decimal places) is _______.
questions.explanationEn: Moles of urea $= \frac{15.0}{60.0} = 0.25\text{ mol}$. Mass of water $= 0.250\text{ kg}$, so molality $m = \frac{0.25}{0.250} = 1.00\text{ mol kg}^{-1}$. For a non-electrolyte ($i = 1$), $\Delta T_f = K_f m = 1.86 \times 1.00 = 1.86\text{ K}$.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Chemical Thermodynamics & Phase Equilibria (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: At $298\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ bar}$, the total volume (in $\text{cm}^3$) of a binary solution containing $n_1\text{ mol}$ of solvent and $n_2\text{ mol}$ of solute is given by $V = 18.0\,n_1 + 58.0\,n_2 + 0.50\,n_2^2$. The partial molar volume of the solute ($\bar{V}_2$, in $\text{cm}^3\text{ mol}^{-1}$, rounded off to one decimal place) at $n_2 = 2.0\text{ mol}$ is _______.
questions.explanationEn: The partial molar volume of the solute is $\bar{V}_2 = \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial n_2}\right)_{T,P,n_1} = \frac{\partial}{\partial n_2}(18.0\,n_1 + 58.0\,n_2 + 0.50\,n_2^2) = 58.0 + 1.00\,n_2$. Evaluating at $n_2 = 2.0\text{ mol}$ gives $\bar{V}_2 = 58.0 + 2.0 = 60.0\text{ cm}^3\text{ mol}^{-1}$.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Chemical Thermodynamics & Phase Equilibria (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: A real gas obeys the Berthelot equation of state $P = \frac{RT}{V_m - b} - \frac{a}{T V_m^2}$. The internal pressure $\pi_T = \left(\frac{\partial U_m}{\partial V_m}\right)_T$ of this gas is:
questions.explanationEn: Using $\pi_T = T\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_{V_m} - P$. Differentiating $P = \frac{RT}{V_m - b} - \frac{a}{T V_m^2}$ with respect to $T$ at constant $V_m$ gives $\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_{V_m} = \frac{R}{V_m - b} + \frac{a}{T^2 V_m^2}$. Multiplying by $T$ and subtracting $P$ yields $\pi_T = \left(\frac{RT}{V_m - b} + \frac{a}{T V_m^2}\right) - \left(\frac{RT}{V_m - b} - \frac{a}{T V_m^2}\right) = \frac{2a}{T V_m^2}$.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Chemical Thermodynamics & Phase Equilibria (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: For an ideal gas-phase reaction with stoichiometric gas mole change $\Delta \nu_g$, the partial derivative $\left(\frac{\partial \ln K_x}{\partial P}\right)_T$ is equal to:
questions.explanationEn:
For ideal gases, $K_p = K_x P^{\Delta 
u_g}$, where $K_p$ depends only on temperature $T$. Taking the natural logarithm gives $\ln K_x = \ln K_p - \Delta 
u_g \ln P$. Differentiating with respect to $P$ at constant $T$ yields $\left( rac{\partial \ln K_x}{\partial P}ight)_T = - rac{\Delta 
u_g}{P}$.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Chemical Thermodynamics & Phase Equilibria (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Applying Euler's theorem for homogeneous functions of degree $1$ to the internal energy $U(S, V, n_1, n_2, \dots)$ yields the integrated form:
questions.explanationEn: Since $U(S, V, \{n_i\})$ is homogeneous of degree $1$ in its extensive natural variables $(S, V, \{n_i\})$, Euler's theorem states $U = S\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial S}\right) + V\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right) + \sum_i n_i\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial n_i}\right) = TS - PV + \sum_i \mu_i n_i$. Note that $G = U - TS + PV = \sum_i \mu_i n_i$.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Chemical Thermodynamics & Phase Equilibria (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: The binary liquid system nicotine-water exhibits a closed-loop miscibility gap with a lower critical solution temperature (LCST) at $60.8\,^\circ\text{C}$ and an upper critical solution temperature (UCST) at $208\,^\circ\text{C}$. Inside the closed loop, the number of liquid phases ($P$) and reduced degrees of freedom ($F'$ at fixed pressure) are, respectively:
questions.explanationEn: Inside the closed miscibility loop (between the LCST and UCST), the mixture splits into two conjugate partially miscible liquid phases ($P = 2$). For a binary condensed system ($C = 2$) at fixed pressure, the reduced phase rule gives $F' = C - P + 1 = 2 - 2 + 1 = 1$. Outside the loop (below $60.8\,^\circ\text{C}$ or above $208\,^\circ\text{C}$), the liquids are completely miscible ($P = 1, F' = 2$).

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Chemical Thermodynamics & Phase Equilibria (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: The Gibbs free energy $G(T, P, n)$ is obtained from the internal energy $U(S, V, n)$ via a double Legendre transformation replacing $(S, V)$ by $(T, P)$. Which expression correctly defines $G$ and its natural-variable differential?
optionsEn: $G = U + TS - PV$ and $dG = S\,dT - V\,dP + \mu\,dn$
questions.explanationEn: Since $T = (\partial U/\partial S)_{V,n}$ and $-P = (\partial U/\partial V)_{S,n}$, the Legendre transform replacing $S$ with $T$ and $V$ with $-P$ is $G = U - TS - (-P)V = U - TS + PV$. Taking the differential and substituting $dU = TdS - PdV + \mu\,dn$ yields $dG = -S\,dT + V\,dP + \mu\,dn$.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Chemical Thermodynamics & Phase Equilibria (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: In a two-component solid-liquid phase diagram ($T$ vs $x_B$ at constant pressure) of components $\text{A}$ and $\text{B}$ that form a single congruently melting compound $\text{AB}$ (with no solid solubility), which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?
optionsEn: The diagram can be viewed as two simple eutectic diagrams side-by-side: $\text{A}-\text{AB}$ and $\text{AB}-\text{B}$.
There are two distinct eutectic points in the phase diagram.
At the congruent melting point of $\text{AB}$, the liquid and solid $\text{AB}$ have the exact same composition ($x_B = 0.5$).
At the congruent melting point of $\text{AB}$, the reduced degrees of freedom $F'$ equals $1$.
questions.explanationEn: A congruently melting compound $\text{AB}$ melts cleanly to a liquid of identical composition ($x_B = 0.5$, C), dividing the binary diagram into two independent simple eutectic subsystems, $\text{A}-\text{AB}$ and $\text{AB}-\text{B}$ (A), with two eutectic points (B). At the congruent melting point, the constraint $x_{\text{s}} = x_{\text{l}} = 0.5$ makes the system effectively single-component ($C_{\text{eff}} = 1$) with $P = 2$, so $F' = 1 - 2 + 1 = 0$ (invariant, D is false).

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Chemical Thermodynamics & Phase Equilibria (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: When a non-volatile solute is dissolved in a pure liquid solvent to form a dilute ideal solution, which of the following thermodynamic statements is/are CORRECT?
optionsEn: The chemical potential of the solvent in the solution is lowered by $-RT\ln(1/x_1) = RT\ln x_1 < 0$.
The ebullioscopic constant $K_b$ is given by $\frac{R M_1 T_b^{*2}}{1000\,\Delta_{\text{vap}} H_m}$ (with $M_1$ in $\text{g mol}^{-1}$).
The freezing point is depressed because the solute lowers the chemical potential of the liquid solvent while the pure solid solvent's chemical potential is unchanged.
Both $K_b$ and $K_f$ depend strongly on the chemical identity of the non-volatile solute.
questions.explanationEn: In an ideal solution, $\mu_1 = \mu_1^* + RT\ln x_1 < \mu_1^*$ since $x_1 < 1$ (A). Because the pure solid solvent's $\mu_1(\text{s})$ is unaffected while $\mu_1(\text{l})$ shifts downward, the solid-liquid intersection shifts to a lower temperature (C). Standard derivation gives $K_b = \frac{R M_1 T_b^{*2}}{1000\,\Delta_{\text{vap}} H_m}$ (B), which depends solely on the properties of the solvent, not the solute (D is false).

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Chemical Thermodynamics & Phase Equilibria (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: The normal boiling point of water at $1.00\text{ atm}$ is $373.15\text{ K}$, and its molar enthalpy of vaporization is $40.66\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. Assuming $\Delta_{\text{vap}} H_m$ is constant, the boiling point of water at $0.50\text{ atm}$ (in $\text{K}$, rounded off to one decimal place) is _______. (Given: $R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$)
questions.explanationEn: By the integrated Clausius-Clapeyron equation, $\ln\left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right) = -\frac{\Delta_{\text{vap}} H_m}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}\right)$. Substituting $P_2/P_1 = 0.50$: $\frac{1}{T_2} = \frac{1}{373.15} - \frac{8.314}{40660}\ln(0.50) = 2.67989 \times 10^{-3} + 1.4173 \times 10^{-4} = 2.82162 \times 10^{-3}\text{ K}^{-1}$, giving $T_2 = 354.4\text{ K}$.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Chemical Thermodynamics & Phase Equilibria (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: At $300\text{ K}$, the second virial coefficient of a gas is $B = -120\text{ cm}^3\text{ mol}^{-1}$. Using the truncated virial equation $Z = 1 + \frac{BP}{RT}$, the fugacity of the gas at $P = 20.0\text{ bar}$ (in $\text{bar}$, rounded off to two decimal places) is _______. (Given: $R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$, $1\text{ bar} = 10^5\text{ Pa}$)
questions.explanationEn: For $Z = 1 + \frac{BP}{RT}$, $\ln\phi = \int_0^P \frac{Z-1}{P'}\,dP' = \frac{BP}{RT}$. Converting units: $B = -1.20 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^3\text{ mol}^{-1}$ and $P = 2.0 \times 10^6\text{ Pa}$, so $\ln\phi = \frac{(-1.20 \times 10^{-4})(2.0 \times 10^6)}{8.314 \times 300} = -0.096223$. Thus $\phi = e^{-0.096223} = 0.90826$, and fugacity $f = \phi P = 0.90826 \times 20.0 = 18.17\text{ bar}$.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Chemical Thermodynamics & Phase Equilibria (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Two solids $\text{A}$ and $\text{B}$ form a simple binary eutectic system with ideal liquid solutions and zero solid solubility. Both pure $\text{A}$ and pure $\text{B}$ have identical melting points $T_m^* = 350.0\text{ K}$ and identical molar enthalpies of fusion $\Delta_{\text{fus}} H_m = 16.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. The eutectic temperature ($T_e$, in $\text{K}$, rounded off to one decimal place) is _______. (Given: $R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$)
questions.explanationEn: By symmetry, since $\text{A}$ and $\text{B}$ have identical $T_m^*$ and $\Delta_{\text{fus}} H_m$, the eutectic composition is equimolar ($x_A = x_B = 0.50$). Applying the ideal solubility (Schröder-van Laar) equation $\ln x_A = -\frac{\Delta_{\text{fus}} H_m}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_e} - \frac{1}{T_m^*}\right)$: $\frac{1}{T_e} = \frac{1}{350.0} - \frac{8.314}{16000}\ln(0.50) = 2.85714 \times 10^{-3} + 3.6018 \times 10^{-4} = 3.21732 \times 10^{-3}\text{ K}^{-1}$, yielding $T_e = 310.8\text{ K}$.
